# Scenario benchmark — one machine, multiple cores (v0.3.2)

ONE multi-process test · two rate settings on 10-second windows · 3 repeats each, median highlighted. Engines: dripline
(pure Python) → Python rivals → **governor (Rust, always present)**.
4 worker processes on 4 pinned cores, 100 clients round-robin per worker, max-speed load for 20 s per repeat. Rivals hold one private limiter per worker (the classic Redis-less model); dripline-arena workers map ONE shared arena file (the v0.2 model) — per-client budgets are global.

Environment: 3.12.14 · AMD Ryzen 5 3600X 6-Core Processor · Linux-6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.41

## Rate setting LOOSE — 1000 admits per 10 s per client

Theoretical admit ceiling per client over 20 s: ~3000 (burst + sustained). Admits far below it mean the
engine rejected everything beyond budget; admits above it would be a bug.

|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| dripline-apex | 9,551,950 / 9,237,700 / 9,422,150 | **9,422,150** | 301,724 | 0.16% | 1482 |
| governor-rust | 66,763,150 / 66,301,150 / 66,434,800 | **66,434,800** | 1,199,600 | 0.09% | 2999 |

## Notes

- Worker count = core count; every engine faces the identical client cycle
  and duration. Driver clock checks are amortized (1 per 1000 decisions).
- FAST protocol (20 s per repeat); release runs use 60 s
- governor runs the same scenario via its --scenario-worker mode: identical
  quota semantics (unit period = window/amount, capacity = burst).
- This is throughput + budget compliance under sustained load, not per-call
  latency (that lives in run.py / champions tables).
- Reading the admits column: per-worker engines each enforce their own
  copy, so their TOTAL admits run ~Wx the per-client ceiling; the
  shared-arena row enforces the global budget (~1x ceiling) — the xW
  over-admission the arena exists to fix.
